sections.name: Hook
lines: pw_hook
A well-built website doesn't know your password. Not even the people who run it.
pw_title
Here's the clever trick behind every login, in five steps.

sections.name: The one-way blender
lines: pw_hash
Step one. When you sign up, the site runs your password through a hash. Think of it as a one-way blender.
pw_out
Out comes a scrambled string of characters. The site saves that, and throws your actual password away.
pw_oneway
You can't un-blend a smoothie. In the same way, there's no practical way to turn the hash back into your password.

sections.name: Checking a login
lines: pw_login
Step two. When you log in, the site blends whatever you type, and compares the result with the stored hash.
pw_match
Same password, same hash, you're in. Change a single letter, and the hash comes out completely different.

sections.name: A pinch of salt
lines: pw_same
Step three. If two people chose the same password, they'd get the same hash. That's a clue for attackers.
pw_salt
So sites add a random extra bit, called a salt, before blending. Now every hash is unique, even for identical passwords.

sections.name: Slow on purpose
lines: pw_slow
Step four. Good password hashes are deliberately slow, taking a fraction of a second each.
pw_guess
You won't notice it once. But an attacker trying billions of guesses suddenly needs far, far longer.

sections.name: Your part
lines: pw_weak
Step five. Hashing can't save a password that's easy to guess. Attackers try the common ones first.
pw_tips
So use long, unique passwords, a password manager, and two-factor login. And if a site ever emails you your old password, it wasn't hashing it.

sections.name: Recap
lines: w_recap
Passwords get hashed. Logins compare hashes. Salt makes each one unique, slow hashing stalls attackers, and long, unique passwords do the rest.
outro
Your password is safest when even the website doesn't know it. Follow for more of the tech you use every day.
